name: Archelaus (son of Herod)
title: Ethnarch over Judea, Samaria and Idumea
summary: When Herod the Great died in 4 BC, Emperor Augustus divided his kingdom among three sons. Archelaus, born to Herod and his Samaritan wife Malthace, received the most significant portion – Judea, Samaria, and Idumea – but was granted only the rank of ethnarch, not the royal title he had sought. His rule was marked by brutality and arbitrariness from the very beginning, and it was precisely fear of this ruler that caused Joseph, guided by God in a dream, to take Mary and the child Jesus to Nazareth in Galilee instead of returning to Judea (Matt 2:22–23). Discontent with Archelaus was so widespread that delegations of both Jews and Samaritans traveled to Rome to demand his removal. In 6 AD, Augustus intervened, deposed Archelaus, and exiled him to Gaul. Judea was then placed directly under Roman prefects – an administrative change that had far-reaching consequences for the political landscape in Jesus' time.

keyEvents.title: Archelaus appointed ethnarch over Judea
keyEvents.description: After the death of Herod the Great in 4 BC, Archelaus went to Rome to have his rule confirmed by Emperor Augustus. The emperor divided the kingdom among Herod's sons and gave Archelaus the largest portion—Judea, Samaria and Idumea—but only with the title ethnarch, not king. Matthew nevertheless uses the Greek verb 'basileuei' (reigns as king) to describe his rule, reflecting how the people perceived his actual position of power.

keyEvents.title: Joseph avoids Judea and settles in Nazareth
keyEvents.description: When Joseph learned that Archelaus was ruling over Judea after his father, he feared taking his family there. Warned in a dream, he led Mary and the child Jesus to Galilee and settled in the town of Nazareth, which fell under the milder jurisdiction of Herod Antipas. Matthew links this to a prophetic tradition that the Messiah would be called a Nazarene—an expression likely connected to the Hebrew 'netser' (branch/shoot) from Isaiah 11:1.

versions.summary: Archelaus was the son of Herod the Great and Malthace, and inherited rule over Judea, Samaria and Idumea after his father's death in 4 BC. He was known for his brutal manner of ruling, which caused Joseph to settle in Galilee instead of Judea when the family returned from Egypt.
versions.title: Ethnarch over Judea
versions.reason: [major] Archelaus did not hold the title 'king'. Augustus denied him the royal title and instead gave him the title 'ethnarch'. The role should be corrected to 'ethnarch' for historical accuracy. Although Matt 2:22 uses the verb 'basileuei' (to reign as king), his official title was ethnarch.; [major] Archelaus's mother was Maltake (also spelled Malthake), a Samaritan woman who was one of Herod the Great's wives. This is even mentioned in the summary text but is missing from the family object.; [minor] Archelaus was married to Glaphyra, daughter of King Archelaus of Cappadocia. This marriage was controversial because she had previously been married to his half-brother Alexander. Including this would strengthen the profile.; [minor] The first two events ('Joseph fears Archelaus' and 'Inherits Judea after Herod') overlap significantly, as both refer to Matt 2:22. These could usefully be merged into a single event to avoid redundancy.; [minor] The summary is good but could mention that Archelaus was deposed by the Romans in 6 AD due to his brutal rule and exiled to Gaul. This is an important historical detail that underscores his character.; [minor] The description states that Archelaus became 'king', but he never received the royal title – he became ethnarch. Although the Greek word in Matt 2:22 is 'basileuei', the description should clarify that he ruled (without the title of king) for historical accuracy.; [minor] The phrasing 'the prophecy that Jesus would be called a Nazarene' is disputed. There is no single Old Testament prophecy with this exact wording. Matthew likely refers to a broader prophetic tradition, possibly connected to the Hebrew word 'netser' (shoot/branch) in Isa 11:1. The description should be nuanced.

versions.summary: Archelaus was the son of Herod the Great and Malthace, and took over rule of Judea, Samaria, and Idumea after his father's death in 4 BC. Emperor Augustus gave him the title ethnarch, but denied him the royal title. He was known for his brutal and oppressive rule, which led Joseph to settle in Nazareth in Galilee instead of Judea when the holy family returned from Egypt (Matt 2:22–23). In AD 6, Archelaus was deposed by the Romans following complaints from his subjects and sent into exile in Gaul, after which Judea came under direct Roman rule.

versions.reason: [minor] The summary closely resembles version 1 in structure and content ('son of Herod the Great and Malthace, who took over rule over Judea, Samaria and Idumea...'). It should be rephrased more distinctly to set it apart from the earlier version.; [minor] The two key events overlap significantly – both refer to Matt 2:22-23 and concern Joseph's response to Archelaus' reign. The first event could focus more purely on Archelaus' assumption of power without mentioning Joseph, while the second covers Joseph's reaction.; [minor] The reference to Philip is somewhat ambiguous. Archelaus had a half-brother named Philip (son of Cleopatra of Jerusalem) who became tetrarch, but the full brother (son of Malthace), sometimes called 'Herod Philip', is also mentioned. It may be helpful to clarify which Philip is meant, or possibly include both.; [minor] The role 'ruler' is very general. A more specific title such as 'tetrarch' (even though his actual title was ethnarch) or 'regent' could be considered, perhaps even 'deposed ruler' to capture the full scope of his career.

versions.summary: After Herod the Great died in 4 BC, Emperor Augustus divided his kingdom among three of his sons. Archelaus, who was a son of Herod and the Samaritan Malthace, received the largest portion – Judea, Samaria, and Idumea – but only with the rank of ethnarch, not king. He quickly became notorious for violent and arbitrary rule, and his oppressive governance is the reason Joseph, following divine guidance in a dream, chose to settle with Mary and the child Jesus in Nazareth in Galilee rather than return to Judea (Matt 2:22–23). Archelaus' reputation was so bad that both Jews and Samaritans eventually sent delegations to Rome to request his removal. In 6 AD he was removed from power and exiled to Gaul by Augustus, and Judea was transformed into a Roman province under the direct rule of prefects.

versions.reason: [minor] Philip (Herod Philip) is correct as a half-brother, but it can be clarified that there are several half-brothers (e.g., Herod II/Philip). The current list is acceptable as a simplified presentation of the most well-known full brothers and half-brothers.; [minor] The phrasing 'settled down' should be 'settled down' – but this is correct Norwegian. However, the connection between 'Nazarene' and 'netser' is an interpretation that should be presented cautiously. The current wording is acceptable.; [minor] The role 'builder' could have been added given the footnotes about building projects, but this is a secondary role and not necessary to include.

footnotes.text: The Greek word 'basileuei' (βασιλεύει) in Matt 2:22 means 'reigns as king', but historically Archelaus never received the royal title. Emperor Augustus gave him only the title 'ethnarch' (ruler of a people), with a promise of kingship if he proved worthy – which never happened.

Archelaus was deposed by Emperor Augustus in 6 AD following complaints from Jewish and Samaritan delegations about his brutal rule. He was exiled to Vienne in Gaul (modern-day France), and Judea was then placed under direct Roman rule through prefects – the first being Coponius.

Josephus (Jewish Antiquities 17.13.2) describes how Archelaus began his reign by massacring around 3,000 Jews in the temple during Passover celebrations, confirming the biblical portrayal of him as a brutal ruler Joseph feared.

Maltake (Malthake) was a Samaritan woman and one of Herod the Great's ten wives. She was the mother of both Archelaus and Herod Antipas. Her Samaritan origin may have contributed to the negative attitude Jews held toward Archelaus' rule.

The term 'Nazarene' in Matt 2:23 has been the subject of much discussion. Many scholars link it to the Hebrew word 'netser' (נֵצֶר), meaning 'shoot' or 'branch', used in Isaiah 11:1 about the Messiah. Others have suggested a connection to 'nazir' (consecrated) or to the low status of the town of Nazareth.

Archaeological excavations have revealed that Archelaus continued several of his father's building projects, including the expansion of the winter palace in Jericho and the construction of an aqueduct to palm plantations near the city. This shows he sought to legitimize his power through grand building projects, in line with Herodian tradition.

Archelaus married Glaphyra, daughter of King Archelaus of Cappadocia, who had previously been married to his half-brother Alexander. According to Josephus, this marriage was controversial because it was considered a violation of Jewish law, since Glaphyra had children with his deceased brother.
